{{Short description|Array of numbers describing a metric connection}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2019}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[physics]], the '''Christoffel symbols''' are an array of numbers describing a [[metric connection]].<ref>See, for instance, {{harv|Spivak|1999}} and {{harv|Choquet-Bruhat|DeWitt-Morette|1977}}</ref>  The metric connection is a specialization of the [[affine connection]] to [[surface (topology)|surface]]s or other [[manifold]]s endowed with a [[metric tensor|metric]], allowing distances to be measured on that surface.  In [[differential geometry]], an affine connection can be defined without reference to a metric, and many additional concepts follow: [[parallel transport]], [[covariant derivative]]s, [[geodesic]]s, etc. also do not require the concept of a metric.<ref>Ronald Adler, Maurice Bazin, Menahem Schiffer, ''Introduction to General Relativity'' (1965) McGraw-Hill Book Company {{ISBN|0-07-000423-4}} (''See section 2.1'')</ref><ref>Charles W. Misner, Kip S. Thorne, John Archibald Wheeler, ''Gravitation'' (1973) W. H. Freeman {{ISBN|0-7167-0334-3}} (''See chapters 8-11'')</ref> However, when a metric is available, these concepts can be directly tied to the "shape" of the manifold itself; that shape is determined by how the [[tangent space]] is attached to the [[cotangent space]] by the [[metric tensor]].<ref>Misner, Thorne, Wheeler, ''op. cit.'' (''See chapter 13'')</ref> Abstractly, one would say that the manifold has an associated ([[orthonormal]]) [[frame bundle]], with each "[[vierbein|frame]]" being a possible choice of a [[coordinate frame]]. An invariant metric implies that the [[structure group]] of the frame bundle is the [[orthogonal group]] {{math|O(''p'', ''q'')}}. As a result, such a manifold is necessarily a ([[pseudo-Riemannian manifold|pseudo-]])[[Riemannian manifold]].<ref>Jurgen Jost, ''Riemannian Geometry and Geometric Analysis'', (2002) Springer-Verlag {{ISBN|3-540-42627-2}}</ref><ref>David Bleeker, ''Gauge Theory and Variational Principles'' (1991) Addison-Wesely Publishing Company {{ISBN|0-201-10096-7}}</ref> The Christoffel symbols provide a concrete representation of the connection of (pseudo-)[[Riemannian geometry]] in terms of coordinates on the manifold. Additional concepts, such as parallel transport, geodesics, etc. can then be expressed in terms of Christoffel symbols.

In general, there are an infinite number of metric connections for a given [[metric tensor]]; however, there is a unique connection that is free of [[torsion tensor|torsion]], the [[Levi-Civita connection]]. It is common in physics and [[general relativity]] to work almost exclusively with the Levi-Civita connection, by working in [[coordinate frame]]s (called [[Holonomic basis|holonomic coordinates]]) where the torsion vanishes. For example, in [[Euclidean spaces]], the Christoffel symbols describe how the [[Curvilinear coordinates#Covariant and contravariant bases|local coordinate bases]] change from point to point.

At each point of the underlying {{math|''n''}}-dimensional manifold, for any local coordinate system around that point, the Christoffel symbols are denoted {{math|Γ<sup>''i''</sup><sub>''jk''</sub>}} for {{math|1=''i'', ''j'', ''k'' = 1, 2, ..., ''n''}}. Each entry of this {{math|''n'' × ''n'' × ''n''}} [[Matrix (mathematics)|array]] is a [[real number]]. Under ''linear'' [[coordinate transformations]] on the manifold, the Christoffel symbols transform like the components of a [[tensor]], but under general coordinate transformations ([[diffeomorphism]]s) they do not.  Most of the algebraic properties of the Christoffel symbols follow from their relationship to the affine connection; only a few follow from the fact that the [[structure group]] is the orthogonal group {{math|O(''m'', ''n'')}} (or the [[Lorentz group]] {{math|O(3, 1)}} for general relativity).

Christoffel symbols are used for performing practical calculations. For example, the [[Riemann curvature tensor]] can be expressed entirely in terms of the Christoffel symbols and their first [[partial derivative]]s. In [[general relativity]], the connection plays the role of the [[gravitational force field]] with the corresponding [[gravitational potential]] being the metric tensor. When the coordinate system and the metric tensor share some symmetry, many of the {{math|Γ<sup>''i''</sup><sub>''jk''</sub>}} are [[0 (number)|zero]].

The Christoffel symbols are named for [[Elwin Bruno Christoffel]] (1829–1900).<ref name="christoffel" >{{citation|title=Ueber die Transformation der homogenen Differentialausdrücke zweiten Grades|last=Christoffel|first=E.B.|author-link=Elwin Bruno Christoffel |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik|volume=70|pages=46–70|year=1869|url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?PPN=GDZPPN002153882&IDDOC=266356}}</ref>

==Note==
<!--'Connection coefficient' and 'Connection coefficients' and redirect here-->
The definitions given below are valid for both [[Riemannian manifold]]s and [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s, such as those of [[general relativity]], with careful distinction being made between upper and lower indices ([[covariance and contravariance of vectors|contra-variant and co-variant]] indices). The formulas hold for either [[sign convention]], unless otherwise noted.

[[Einstein notation|Einstein summation convention]] is used in this article, with vectors indicated by bold font. The '''connection coefficients'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> of the [[Levi-Civita connection]] (or pseudo-Riemannian connection) expressed in a coordinate basis are called ''Christoffel symbols''.

==Preliminary definitions==
{{main|Tangent space}}
Given a [[manifold]] <math>M</math>, an [[atlas (topology)|atlas]] consists of a collection of charts <math>\varphi: U \to \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> for each [[open cover]] <math>U\subset M</math>. Such charts allow the standard [[vector basis]] <math>(\vec{e}_1,\cdots,\vec{e}_n)</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> to be [[pullback (differential geometry)|pulled back]] to a vector basis on the tangent space <math>TM</math> of <math>M</math>. This is done as follows. Given some arbitrary real function <math>f:M\to\mathbb{R}</math>, the chart allows a [[gradient]] to be defined:

:<math>\partial_i f \equiv \frac{\partial \left(f\circ\varphi^{-1}\right)}{\partial x^i}\quad\mbox{for } i = 1,\, 2,\, \dots,\, n</math>

This gradient is commonly called a [[pullback]] because it "pulls back" the gradient on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> to a gradient on <math>M</math>. The pullback is independent of the chart <math>\varphi</math>. In this way, the standard vector basis <math>(\vec{e}_1,\cdots,\vec{e}_n)</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> pulls back to a standard ("coordinate") vector basis <math>(\partial_1,\cdots,\partial_n)</math> on <math>TM</math>. This is called the "coordinate basis", because it explicitly depends on the coordinates on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. It is sometimes called the "local basis".

This definition allows a common [[abuse of notation]]. The <math>\partial_i</math> were defined to be in one-to-one correspondence with the basis vectors <math>\vec{e}_i</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. The notation <math>\partial_i</math> serves as a reminder that the basis vectors on the tangent space <math>TM</math> came from a gradient construction. Despite this, it is common to "forget" this construction, and just write (or rather, define) vectors <math>e_i</math> on <math>TM</math> such that <math>e_i \equiv \partial_i</math>. The full range of commonly used notation includes the use of arrows and boldface to denote vectors:

:<math>\partial_i \equiv \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \equiv e_i \equiv \vec{e}_i \equiv \mathbf{e}_i \equiv \boldsymbol\partial_i</math>

where <math>\equiv</math> is used as a reminder that these are defined to be equivalent notation for the same concept. The choice of notation is according to style and taste, and varies from text to text.

The coordinate basis provides a vector basis for [[vector field]]s on <math>M</math>. Commonly used notation for vector fields on <math>M</math> include 
:<math>X = \vec X = X^i\partial_i=X^i\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}</math>
The upper-case <math>X</math>, without the vector-arrow, is particularly popular for [[Abstract index notation|index-free notation]], because it both minimizes clutter and reminds that results are independent of the chosen basis, and, in this case, independent of the atlas. 

The same abuse of notation is used to [[pushforward (differential)|push forward]] [[one-form]]s from <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> to <math>M</math>. This is done by writing <math>(\varphi^1,\ldots, \varphi^n)=(x^{1},\ldots,x^{n})</math> or <math>x=\varphi</math> or <math>x^i=\varphi^i</math>. The one-form is then <math>dx^i=d\varphi^i</math>. This is soldered to the basis vectors as <math>dx^i(\partial_j)=\delta^i_j</math>. Note the careful use of upper and lower indexes, to distinguish contravariant and covariant vectors.

The pullback induces (defines) a [[metric tensor]] on <math>M</math>. Several styles of notation are commonly used:
<math display="block">g_{ij} = \mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j=\langle \vec{e}_i, \vec{e}_j\rangle = e_i^a e_j^b \,\eta_{ab}</math>
where both the centerdot and the angle-bracket <math>\langle,\rangle</math> denote the [[scalar product]]. The last form uses the [[tensor]] <math>\eta_{ab}</math>, which is understood to be the "flat-space" metric tensor. For [[Riemannian manifold]]s, it is the [[Kronecker delta]] <math>\eta_{ab}=\delta_{ab}</math>. For [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s, it is the [[diagonal matrix]] having signature <math>(p,q)</math>. The notation <math>e_i^a</math> serves as a reminder that pullback really is a linear transform, given as the gradient, above. The index letters <math>a,b,c,\cdots</math> live in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> while the index letters <math>i,j,k,\cdots</math> live in the tangent manifold.

The [[matrix inverse]] <math>g^{ij}</math> of the metric tensor <math>g_{ij}</math> is given by
<math display="block">g^{ij} g_{jk}=\delta^i_k</math>
This is used to define the dual basis:
<math display="block">\mathbf{e}^i = \mathbf{e}_j g^{ji},\quad i = 1,\, 2,\, \dots,\, n</math>

Some texts write <math>\mathbf{g}_i</math> for <math>\mathbf{e}_i</math>, so that the metric tensor takes the particularly beguiling form <math>g_{ij} = \mathbf{g}_i \cdot \mathbf{g}_j</math>. This is commonly done so that the symbol <math>e_i</math> can be used unambiguously for the [[vierbein]].

==Definition in Euclidean space==
In [[Euclidean space]], the general definition given below for the Christoffel symbols of the second kind can be proven to be equivalent to:
<math display="block">{\Gamma^k}_{ij}
  = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{j}}{\partial x^i} \cdot \mathbf{e}^{k}
  = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{j}}{\partial x^i} \cdot g^{km} \mathbf{e}_{m}
</math>

Christoffel symbols of the first kind can then be found via [[Raising and lowering indices|index lowering]]:
<math display="block">\Gamma_{kij}
  = {\Gamma^m}_{ij}g_{mk}
  = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{j}}{\partial x^i} \cdot \mathbf{e}^{m} g_{mk}
  = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{j}}{\partial x^i} \cdot \mathbf{e}_{k}
</math>

Rearranging, we see that (assuming the partial derivative belongs to the tangent space, which cannot occur on a non-Euclidean [[curvature|curved]] space):
<math display="block">\frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{j}}{\partial x^i} = {\Gamma^k}_{ij} \mathbf{e}_{k} = \Gamma_{kij} \mathbf{e}^{k}</math>

In words, the arrays represented by the Christoffel symbols track how the basis changes from point to point. If the derivative does not lie on the tangent space, the right expression is the projection of the derivative over the tangent space (see [[#Covariant derivatives of tensors|covariant derivative]] below). Symbols of the second kind decompose the change with respect to the basis, while symbols of the first kind decompose it with respect to the dual basis. In this form, it is easy to see the symmetry of the lower or last two indices:
<math display="block">{\Gamma^k}_{ij} = {\Gamma^k}_{ji} </math> and <math>\Gamma_{kij} = \Gamma_{kji},</math>
from the definition of <math> \mathbf{e}_i </math> and the fact that partial derivatives commute (as long as the manifold and coordinate system [[Symmetry of second derivatives|are well behaved]]).

The same numerical values for Christoffel symbols of the second kind also relate to derivatives of the dual basis, as seen in the expression:
<math display="block">\frac{\partial \mathbf{e}^{i}}{\partial x^j} = -{\Gamma^i}_{jk} \mathbf{e}^{k},</math>
which we can rearrange as:
<math display="block">{\Gamma^i}_{jk} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{e}^{i}}{\partial x^j} \cdot \mathbf{e}_{k}.</math>

== General definition==
The Christoffel symbols come in two forms: the first kind, and the second kind. The definition of the second kind is more basic, and thus is presented first. 

===Christoffel symbols of the second kind (symmetric definition)===
The Christoffel symbols of the second kind are the connection coefficients—in a coordinate basis—of the [[Levi-Civita connection]].
In other words, the Christoffel symbols of the second kind<ref name="Chatterjee"/><ref name="wolfram2ndkind" /> {{math|Γ<sup>''k''</sup><sub>''ij''</sub>}} (sometimes {{math|Γ{{su|p=''k''|b=''ij''}}}} or {{math|<big>{</big>{{su|p=''k''|b=''ij''}}<big>}</big>}})<ref name="christoffel"/><ref name="Chatterjee"/> are defined as the unique coefficients such that
<math display="block">\nabla_i \mathrm{e}_j = {\Gamma^k}_{ij}\mathrm{e}_k,</math>
where <math>\nabla_i</math> is the [[Levi-Civita connection]] on {{math|''M''}} taken in the coordinate direction {{math|e<sub>''i''</sub>}} (i.e., {{math|∇<sub>''i''</sub> ≡ ∇<sub>e<sub>''i''</sub></sub>}}) and where <math>e_i=\partial_i</math> is a local coordinate ([[holonomic basis|holonomic]]) [[basis of a vector space|basis]]. Since this connection has zero [[Torsion tensor|torsion]], and holonomic vector fields commute (i.e. <math> [e_i, e_j] = [\partial_i, \partial_j] = 0</math>) we have
<math display="block">\nabla_i \mathrm{e}_j = \nabla_j \mathrm{e}_i.</math>
Hence in this basis the connection coefficients are symmetric:<ref name="Chatterjee">{{cite book | first1=U. | last1 = Chatterjee | first2 = N. | last2= Chatterjee | title=Vector & Tensor Analysis | year=2010 | page=480 }}</ref>
<math display="block">{\Gamma^k}_{ij} = {\Gamma^k}_{ji}.</math>
For this reason, a torsion-free connection is often called ''symmetric''.

The Christoffel symbols can be derived from the vanishing of the [[covariant derivative]] of the [[metric tensor]] <math>g_{ik}</math>:
<math display="block">
  0 = \nabla_l g_{ik}
    = \frac{\partial g_{ik}}{\partial x^l} - g_{mk}{\Gamma^m}_{il} - g_{im}{\Gamma^m}_{kl}
    = \frac{\partial g_{ik}}{\partial x^l} - 2g_{m(k}{\Gamma^m}_{i)l}.
</math>

As a shorthand notation, the [[nabla symbol]] and the partial derivative symbols are frequently dropped, and instead a [[semicolon]] and a [[comma]] are used to set off the index that is being used for the derivative.  Thus, the above is sometimes written as
<math display="block">0 = \,g_{ik;l} = g_{ik,l} - g_{mk} {\Gamma^m}_{il} - g_{im} {\Gamma^m}_{kl} .</math>

Using that the symbols are symmetric in the lower two indices, one can solve explicitly for the Christoffel symbols as a function of the metric tensor by permuting the indices and resumming:<ref name="bishopgoldberg" />
<math display="block">{\Gamma^i}_{kl}
  = \frac{1}{2} g^{im} \left(\frac{\partial g_{mk}}{\partial x^l} + \frac{\partial g_{ml}}{\partial x^k} - \frac{\partial g_{kl}}{\partial x^m} \right)
  = \frac{1}{2} g^{im} \left(g_{mk,l} + g_{ml,k} - g_{kl,m}\right),
</math>

where {{math|(''g<sup>jk</sup>'')}} is the inverse of the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] {{math|(''g<sub>jk</sub>'')}}, defined as (using the [[Kronecker delta]], and [[Einstein notation]] for summation) <math>g^{ji}g_{ik}=\delta^j{}_k</math>. Although the Christoffel symbols are written in the same notation as [[Classical treatment of tensors|tensors with index notation]], they do not transform like tensors under [[#Transformation law under change of variable|a change of coordinates]].

====Contraction of indices====
Contracting the upper index with either of the lower indices (those being symmetric) leads to
<math display="block">{\Gamma^{i}}_{ki} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k} \ln\sqrt{|g|}</math>
where <math>g = \det g_{ik}</math> is the determinant of the metric tensor. This identity can be used to evaluate the divergence of vectors and the covariant derivatives of [[tensor density|tensor densities]]. Also 

:<math> {\Gamma^i}_{ki} = {\Gamma^i}_{ik} = \tfrac12 \left( g^{mi} g_{mk,i} + g^{mi} g_{mi,k} - g^{im} g_{ki,m} \right) = \tfrac12 g^{mi} g_{mi,k} </math> .

===Christoffel symbols of the first kind===
The Christoffel symbols of the first kind can be derived either from the Christoffel symbols of the second kind and the metric,<ref name="ludvigsen">{{citation |last1=Ludvigsen |first1=Malcolm|title=General Relativity: A Geometrical Approach | year=1999|page=88}}</ref>
<math display="block">\Gamma_{cab} = g_{cd} {\Gamma^d}_{ab}\,,</math>

or from the metric alone,<ref name="ludvigsen" />
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\Gamma_{cab}
  &= \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\partial g_{ca}}{\partial x^b} + \frac{\partial g_{cb}}{\partial x^a} - \frac{\partial g_{ab}}{\partial x^c} \right) \\
  &= \frac{1}{2}\, \left(g_{ca, b} + g_{cb, a} - g_{ab, c}\right) \\
  &= \frac{1}{2}\, \left(\partial_{b}g_{ca} + \partial_{a}g_{cb} - \partial_{c}g_{ab}\right) \,.  \\ 
\end{align}
</math>

As an alternative notation one also finds<ref name="christoffel"/><ref name="Chatterjeep114">{{cite book
 |first1=U. |last1=Chatterjee
 |first2=N. |last2=Chatterjee
 |year=2010
 |title=Vector and Tensor Analysis
 |page=480}}</ref><ref name="dirkstruik">{{cite book
 |first1=D.J. |last1=Struik |author-link=Dirk Jan Struik
 |title=Lectures on Classical Differential Geometry
 |edition= first published in 1988 Dover
 |year=1961
 |page=114
}}</ref>

<math display="block">\Gamma_{cab} = [ab, c].</math>
It is worth noting that {{math|1=[''ab'', ''c''] = [''ba'', ''c'']}}.<ref name="bishopgoldberg" >{{citation | last1=Bishop|first1=R.L.|last2=Goldberg| title = Tensor Analysis on Manifolds| year=1968|page=241}}</ref>

===Connection coefficients in a nonholonomic basis===
The Christoffel symbols are most typically defined in a coordinate basis, which is the convention followed here. In other words, the name '''Christoffel symbols''' is reserved only for coordinate (i.e., [[holonomic basis|holonomic]]) frames. However, the connection coefficients can also be defined in an arbitrary (i.e., nonholonomic) basis of tangent vectors {{math|'''u'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} by
<math display="block">\nabla_{\mathbf{u}_j}\mathbf{u}_i = {\omega^k}_{ij}\mathbf{u}_k.</math>

Explicitly, in terms of the metric tensor, this is<ref name="wolfram2ndkind">{{cite web |url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ChristoffelSymboloftheSecondKind.html. |title= Christoffel Symbol of the Second Kind -- from Wolfram MathWorld|website=mathworld.wolfram.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123011440/http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ChristoffelSymboloftheSecondKind.html |archive-date=2009-01-23}}</ref>
<math display="block">{\omega^i}_{kl} = \frac{1}{2} g^{im} \left( g_{mk,l} + g_{ml,k} - g_{kl,m} + c_{mkl} + c_{ml k} - c_{kl m} \right),</math>

where {{math|1=''c<sub>klm</sub>'' = ''g<sub>mp</sub>c<sub>kl</sub><sup>p</sup>''}} are the [[Commutator (ring theory)|commutation coefficients]] of the basis; that is,
<math display="block">[\mathbf{u}_k,\, \mathbf{u}_l] = {c_{kl}}^m \mathbf{u}_m</math>

where {{math|'''u'''<sub>''k''</sub>}} are the basis [[vector space|vector]]s and {{math|[ , ]}} is the [[Lie derivative|Lie bracket]]. The standard unit vectors in [[vector fields in cylindrical and spherical coordinates|spherical and cylindrical coordinates]] furnish an example of a basis with non-vanishing commutation coefficients. The difference between the connection in such a frame, and the Levi-Civita connection is known as the [[contorsion tensor]].

===Ricci rotation coefficients (asymmetric definition)===
When we choose the basis {{math|'''X'''<sub>''i''</sub> ≡ '''u'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} orthonormal: {{math|1=''g<sub>ab</sub>'' ≡ ''η<sub>ab</sub>'' = ⟨''X<sub>a</sub>'', ''X<sub>b</sub>''⟩}} then {{math|1=''g<sub>mk,l</sub>'' ≡ ''η<sub>mk,l</sub>'' = 0}}. This implies that
<math display="block">{\omega^i}_{kl} = \frac{1}{2} \eta^{im} \left( c_{mkl} + c_{ml k} - c_{kl m} \right)</math>
and the connection coefficients become antisymmetric in the first two indices:
<math display="block">\omega_{abc} = -\omega_{bac}\,,</math>
where
<math display="block">\omega_{abc} = \eta_{ad}{\omega^d}_{bc}\, .</math>

In this case, the connection coefficients {{math|''ω<sup>a</sup><sub>bc</sub>''}} are called the '''Ricci rotation coefficients'''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Dei sistemi di congruenze ortogonali in una varietà qualunque|author=G. Ricci-Curbastro |journal=Mem. Acc. Lincei |volume=2|year=1896|pages=276–322|issue=5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Ricci's coefficients of rotation |author=H. Levy|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=31|year=1925|pages=142–145| issue=3–4| url=http://projecteuclid.org/DPubS?service=UI&version=1.0&verb=Display&handle=euclid.bams/1183486405|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1925-03996-8| doi-access=free}}</ref>

Equivalently, one can define Ricci rotation coefficients as follows:<ref name="wolfram2ndkind" />
<math display="block">{\omega^k}_{ij} := \mathbf{u}^k \cdot \left( \nabla_j \mathbf{u}_i \right)\,,</math>
where {{math|'''u'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is an orthonormal nonholonomic basis and {{math|1='''u'''<sup>''k''</sup> = ''η<sup>kl</sup>'''''u'''<sub>''l''</sub>}} its ''co-basis''.

==Transformation law under change of variable==
Under a change of variable from <math>\left(x^1,\, \ldots,\, x^n\right)</math> to <math>\left(\bar{x}^1,\, \ldots,\, \bar{x}^n\right)</math>, Christoffel symbols transform as

<math display="block">{\bar{\Gamma}^i}_{kl} =
  \frac{\partial \bar{x}^i}{\partial x^m}\,
  \frac{\partial x^n}{\partial \bar{x}^k}\,
  \frac{\partial x^p}{\partial \bar{x}^l}\,
  {\Gamma^m}_{np}
  +
  \frac{\partial^2 x^m}{\partial \bar{x}^k \partial \bar{x}^l}\,
  \frac{\partial \bar{x}^i}{\partial x^m}
</math>

where the overline denotes the Christoffel symbols in the <math>\bar{x}^i</math> coordinate system. The Christoffel symbol does '''not''' transform as a tensor, but rather as an object in the [[jet bundle]]. More precisely, the Christoffel symbols can be considered as functions on the jet bundle of the frame bundle of {{math|''M''}}, independent of any local coordinate system. Choosing a local coordinate system determines a local section of this bundle, which can then be used to pull back the Christoffel symbols to functions on {{math|''M''}}, though of course these functions then depend on the choice of local coordinate system.

For each point, there exist coordinate systems in which the Christoffel symbols vanish at the point.<ref>This is assuming that the connection is symmetric (e.g., the Levi-Civita connection).  If the connection has [[torsion tensor|torsion]], then only the symmetric part of the Christoffel symbol can be made to vanish.</ref>  These are called (geodesic) [[normal coordinates]], and are often used in [[Riemannian geometry]].

There are some interesting properties which can be derived directly from the transformation law.
* For linear transformation, the inhomogeneous part of the transformation (second term on the right-hand side) vanishes identically and then <math>{\Gamma^i}_{jk}</math> behaves like a tensor.
* If we have two fields of connections, say <math>{\Gamma^i}_{jk}</math> and <math>{\tilde\Gamma^i}_{jk}</math>, then their difference <math>{\Gamma^i}_{jk} - {\tilde\Gamma^i}_{jk}</math> is a tensor since the inhomogeneous terms cancel each other. The inhomogeneous terms depend only on how the coordinates are changed, but are independent of Christoffel symbol itself.
* If the Christoffel symbol is unsymmetric about its lower indices in one coordinate system i.e., <math>{\Gamma^i}_{jk} \neq {\Gamma^i}_{kj}</math>, then they remain unsymmetric under any change of coordinates. A corollary to this property is that it is impossible to find a coordinate system in which all elements of Christoffel symbol are zero at a point, unless lower indices are symmetric. This property was pointed out by [[Albert Einstein]]<ref>{{cite web | url =https://archive.org/details/B-001-001-738/page/n0 | title =The Meaning of Relativity (1956, 5th Edition)| last =Einstein | first =Albert | year =2005| publisher = Princeton University Press (2005)}}</ref> and [[Erwin Schrödinger]]<ref>Schrödinger, E. (1950). Space-time structure. Cambridge University Press.</ref> independently.

==Relationship to parallel transport and derivation of Christoffel symbols in Riemannian space==
If a vector <math>\xi^i</math> is transported parallel on a curve parametrized by some parameter <math>s</math> on a [[Riemannian manifold]], the rate of change of the components of the vector is given by
<math display="block">\frac{d\xi^i}{ds} = -{\Gamma^i}_{mj} \frac{dx^m}{ds}\xi^j.</math>

Now just by using the condition that the scalar product <math>g_{ik}\xi^i\eta^k</math> formed by two arbitrary vectors <math>\xi^i</math> and <math>\eta^k</math> is unchanged is enough to derive the Christoffel symbols. The condition is
<math display="block">\frac{d}{ds}\left(g_{ik}\xi^i\eta^k\right) = 0</math>
which by the [[product rule]] expands to
<math display="block">\frac{\partial g_{ik}}{\partial x^l} \frac{dx^l}{ds} \xi^i\eta^k + g_{ik} \frac{d\xi^i}{ds}\eta^k + g_{ik}\xi^i\frac{d\eta^k}{ds} = 0.</math>

Applying the parallel transport rule for the two arbitrary vectors and relabelling dummy indices and collecting the coefficients of <math>\xi^i\eta^k dx^l</math> (arbitrary), we obtain

<math display="block">\frac{\partial g_{ik}}{\partial x^l} = g_{rk}{\Gamma^r}_{il} + g_{ir}{\Gamma^r}_{lk}.</math>

This is same as the equation obtained by requiring the covariant derivative of the metric tensor to vanish in the General definition section. The derivation from here is simple. By cyclically permuting the indices <math>ikl</math> in above equation, we can obtain two more equations and then linearly combining these three equations, we can express <math>{\Gamma^i}_{jk}</math> in terms of the metric tensor.

==Relationship to index-free notation==
Let {{math|''X''}} and {{math|''Y''}} be [[vector fields]] with components {{math|''X<sup>i</sup>''}} and {{math|''Y<sup>k</sup>''}}. Then the {{math|''k''}}th component of the covariant derivative of {{math|''Y''}} with respect to {{math|''X''}} is given by
<math display="block">\left(\nabla_X Y\right)^k = X^i (\nabla_i Y)^k = X^i \left(\frac{\partial Y^k}{\partial x^i} + {\Gamma^k}_{im} Y^m\right).</math>

Here, the [[Einstein notation]] is used, so repeated indices indicate summation over indices and contraction with the metric tensor serves to raise and lower indices:
<math display="block">g(X, Y) = X^i Y_i = g_{ik}X^i Y^k = g^{ik}X_i Y_k.</math>

Keep in mind that {{math|''g<sub>ik</sub>'' ≠ ''g<sup>ik</sup>''}} and that {{math|1=''g<sup>i</sup><sub>k</sub>'' = ''δ&thinsp;<sup>i</sup><sub>k</sub>''}}, the [[Kronecker delta]]. The convention is that the metric tensor is the one with the lower indices; the correct way to obtain {{math|''g<sup>ik</sup>''}} from {{math|''g<sub>ik</sub>''}} is to solve the linear equations {{math|1=''g<sup>ij</sup>g<sub>jk</sub>'' = ''δ&thinsp;<sup>i</sup><sub>k</sub>''}}.

The statement that the connection is [[torsion tensor|torsion]]-free, namely that
<math display="block">\nabla_X Y - \nabla_Y X = [X,\, Y]</math>

is equivalent to the statement that—in a coordinate basis—the Christoffel symbol is symmetric in the lower two indices:
<math display="block">{\Gamma^i}_{jk} = {\Gamma^i}_{kj}.</math>

The index-less transformation properties of a tensor are given by [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullbacks]] for covariant indices, and [[pushforward (differential)|pushforwards]] for contravariant indices. The article on [[Covariant derivative#Coordinate description|covariant derivatives]] provides additional discussion of the correspondence between index-free notation and indexed notation.

==Covariant derivatives of tensors==
The [[covariant derivative]] of a vector field with components {{math|''V<sup>m</sup>''}} is
<math display="block">\nabla_l V^m = \frac{\partial V^m}{\partial x^l} + {\Gamma^m}_{kl} V^k.</math>

By corollary, divergence of a vector can be obtained as
<math display="block">\nabla_i V^i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\partial \left(\sqrt{-g}\, V^i\right)}{\partial x^i}.</math>

The covariant derivative of a [[covector]] field {{math|''ω<sub>m</sub>''}} is
<math display="block">\nabla_l \omega_m = \frac{\partial \omega_m}{\partial x^l} - {\Gamma^k}_{ml} \omega_k.</math>

The symmetry of the Christoffel symbol now implies
<math display="block">\nabla_i\nabla_j \varphi = \nabla_j\nabla_i \varphi</math>
for any scalar field, but in general the covariant derivatives of higher order tensor fields do not commute (see [[Riemann curvature tensor|curvature tensor]]).

The covariant derivative of a type {{math|(2, 0)}} [[tensor]] field {{math|''A<sup>ik</sup>''}} is
<math display="block">\nabla_l A^{ik} = \frac{\partial A^{ik}}{\partial x^l} + {\Gamma^i}_{ml} A^{mk} + {\Gamma^k}_{ml} A^{im},</math>
that is,
<math display="block">{A^{ik}}_{;l} = {A^{ik}}_{,l} + A^{mk} {\Gamma^i}_{ml} + A^{im} {\Gamma^k}_{ml}.</math>

If the tensor field is [[mixed tensor|mixed]] then its covariant derivative is
<math display="block">{A^i}_{k;l} = {A^i}_{k,l} + {A^{m}}_k {\Gamma^i}_{ml} - {A^i}_m {\Gamma^m}_{kl}, </math>
and if the tensor field is of type {{math|(0, 2)}} then its covariant derivative is
<math display="block"> A_{ik;l} = A_{ik,l} - A_{mk} {\Gamma^m}_{il} - A_{im} {\Gamma^m}_{kl}. </math>

===Contravariant derivatives of tensors===
To find the contravariant derivative of a vector field, we must first transform it into a covariant derivative using the metric tensor
<math display="block">\nabla^l V^m = g^{il} \nabla_i V^m = g^{il} \partial_i V^m + g^{il} \Gamma^m_{ki} V^k = \partial^l V^m + g^{il} \Gamma^m_{ki} V^k</math>

==Applications==

===In general relativity===
The Christoffel symbols find frequent use in Einstein's theory of [[general relativity]], where [[spacetime]] is represented by a curved 4-dimensional [[Lorentz manifold]] with a [[Levi-Civita connection]]. The [[Einstein field equations]]—which determine the geometry of spacetime in the presence of matter—contain the [[Ricci tensor]], and so calculating the Christoffel symbols is essential. Once the geometry is determined, the paths of particles and light beams are calculated by solving the [[Geodesics in general relativity|geodesic equations]] in which the Christoffel symbols explicitly appear.

===In classical (non-relativistic) mechanics===
Let <math>x^i</math> be the generalized coordinates and <math>\dot{x}^i</math> be the generalized velocities, then the kinetic energy for a unit mass is given by <math>T = \tfrac{1}{2} g_{ik}\dot{x}^i \dot{x}^k</math>, where <math>g_{ik}</math> is the [[metric tensor]]. If <math>V\left(x^i\right)</math>, the potential function, exists then the contravariant components of the generalized force per unit mass are <math>F_i = \partial V/\partial x^i</math>. The metric (here in a purely spatial domain) can be obtained from the [[line element]] <math>ds^2 = 2T dt^2</math>. Substituting the Lagrangian <math>L = T - V</math> into the [[Euler-Lagrange equation]], we get<ref>Adler, R., Bazin, M., & Schiffer, M. Introduction to General Relativity (New York, 1965).</ref>

<math display="block">g_{ik}\ddot{x}^k + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial g_{ik}}{\partial x^l} + \frac{\partial g_{il}}{\partial x^k} - \frac{\partial g_{lk}}{\partial x^i}\right) \dot{x}^l \dot{x}^k = F_i.</math>

Now multiplying by <math>g^{ij}</math>, we get
<math display="block">\ddot{x}^j + {\Gamma^j}_{lk} \dot{x}^l \dot{x}^k = F^j.</math>

When Cartesian coordinates can be adopted (as in inertial frames of reference), we have an Euclidean metrics, the Christoffel symbol vanishes, and the equation reduces to [[Newton's second law of motion]]. In curvilinear coordinates<ref>David, Kay, ''Tensor Calculus'' (1988) McGraw-Hill Book Company {{ISBN|0-07-033484-6}} (''See section 11.4'')</ref> (forcedly in non-inertial frames, where the metrics is non-Euclidean and not flat), fictitious forces like the [[Centrifugal force]] and [[Coriolis force]] originate from the Christoffel symbols, so from the purely spatial curvilinear coordinates.

===In Earth surface coordinates===
Given a [[spherical coordinate system]], which describes points on the Earth surface (approximated as an ideal sphere).

<math display="block">\begin{align}
x(R, \theta, \varphi) &= \begin{pmatrix} R\cos\theta\cos\varphi & R\cos\theta\sin\varphi & R\sin\theta \end{pmatrix} \\
\end{align}</math>

For a point x, {{mvar|R}} is the distance to the Earth core (usually approximately the [[Earth radius]]). {{mvar|θ}} and {{mvar|φ}} are the [[latitude]] and [[longitude]]. Positive {{mvar|θ}} is the northern hemisphere. To simplify the derivatives, the angles are given in [[radians]] (where d sin(x)/dx = cos(x), the degree values introduce an additional factor of 360 / 2 pi).

At any location, the tangent directions are <math> e_{R}</math> (up), <math> e_{\theta}</math> (north) and <math> e_{\varphi}</math> (east) - you can also use indices 1,2,3.

<math display="block">\begin{align}
e_{R} &= \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\varphi & \cos\theta\sin\varphi & \sin\theta \end{pmatrix} \\
e_{\theta} &= R \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -\sin\theta\cos\varphi & - \sin\theta\sin\varphi & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \\
e_{\varphi} &= R\cos\theta \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -\sin\varphi & \cos\varphi & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\
\end{align}</math>

The related [[metric tensor]] has only diagonal elements (the squared vector lengths). This is an advantage of the coordinate system and not generally true.

<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">\begin{align}
g_{RR} = 1  \qquad &  g_{\theta\theta} = R^2  \qquad &  g_{\varphi\varphi} = R^2\cos^2\theta \qquad & g_{ij} = 0 \quad \mathrm{else} \\
g^{RR} = 1  \qquad &  g^{\theta\theta} = 1/R^2  \qquad &  g^{\varphi\varphi} = 1/(R^2\cos^2\theta) \qquad & g^{ij} = 0 \quad \mathrm{else} \\
\end{align}</math>

Now the necessary quantities can be calculated. Examples:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
e^{R} = e_{R} g^{RR} = 1 \cdot e_{R} &= \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\varphi & \cos\theta\sin\varphi & \sin\theta \end{pmatrix} \\
{\Gamma^R}_{\varphi \varphi} = e^{R} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \varphi} e_\varphi &= e^{R} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -R\cos\theta\cos\varphi & -R\cos\theta\sin\varphi & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -R\cos^2\theta \\
\end{align}</math>

The resulting Christoffel symbols of the second kind <math> {\Gamma^k}_{ji} = e^k \cdot \frac{\partial e_j}{\partial x^i} </math> then are (organized by the "derivative" index {{mvar|i}} in a matrix):

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\begin{pmatrix}
{\Gamma^R}_{RR} & {\Gamma^R}_{\theta R} & {\Gamma^R}_{\varphi R} \\
{\Gamma^\theta }_{RR} & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\theta R} & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\varphi R} \\
{\Gamma^\varphi }_{RR} & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\theta R} & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\varphi R} \\
\end{pmatrix} &= \quad \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/R & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1/R \end{pmatrix} \\
\begin{pmatrix}
{\Gamma^R}_{R\theta } & {\Gamma^R}_{\theta \theta } & {\Gamma^R}_{\varphi \theta } \\
{\Gamma^\theta }_{R\theta } & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\theta \theta } & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\varphi \theta } \\
{\Gamma^\varphi }_{R\theta } & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\theta \theta } & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\varphi \theta } \\
\end{pmatrix} \quad &= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -R & 0 \\ 1/R & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\tan\theta \end{pmatrix} \\
\begin{pmatrix}
{\Gamma^R}_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma^R}_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma^R}_{\varphi \varphi } \\
{\Gamma^\theta }_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma^\theta }_{\varphi \varphi } \\
{\Gamma^\varphi }_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma^\varphi }_{\varphi \varphi } \\
\end{pmatrix} &= \quad \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & -R\cos^2\theta \\ 0 & 0 & \cos\theta\sin\theta \\ 1/R & -\tan\theta & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\
\end{align}</math>

These values show how the tangent directions (columns: <math> e_{R}</math>, <math> e_{\theta}</math>, <math> e_{\varphi}</math>) change, seen from an outside perspective (e.g. from space), but given in the tangent directions of the actual location (rows: {{mvar|R}}, {{mvar|θ}}, {{mvar|φ}}).

As an example, take the nonzero derivatives by {{mvar|θ}} in <math>{\Gamma^k}_{j\ \theta}</math>, which corresponds to a movement towards north (positive dθ):
* The new north direction <math> e_{\theta}</math> changes by -R dθ in the up (R) direction. So the north direction will rotate downwards towards the center of the Earth.
* Similarly, the up direction <math> e_{R}</math> will be adjusted towards the north. The different lengths of <math> e_{R}</math> and <math> e_{\theta}</math> lead to a factor of 1/R .
* Moving north, the east tangent vector <math> e_{\varphi}</math> changes its length (-tan(θ) on the diagonal), it will shrink (-tan(θ) dθ < 0) on the northern hemisphere, and increase (-tan(θ) dθ > 0) on the southern hemisphere.<ref name=":0" />
These effects are maybe not apparent during the movement, because they are the adjustments that keep the measurements in the coordinates {{mvar|R}}, {{mvar|θ}}, {{mvar|φ}}. Nevertheless, it can affect distances, physics equations, etc. So if e.g. you need the exact change of a [[magnetic field]] pointing approximately "south", it can be necessary to also [[Christoffel symbols#Covariant derivatives of tensors|correct]] your measurement by the change of the north direction using the Christoffel symbols to get the "true" ([[tensor]]) value.

The Christoffel symbols of the first kind <math> {\Gamma_l}_{ji} = g_{lk} {\Gamma^k}_{ji} </math> show the same change using metric-corrected coordinates, e.g. for derivative by {{mvar|φ}}:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\begin{pmatrix}
{\Gamma_R}_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma_R}_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma_R}_{\varphi \varphi } \\
{\Gamma_\theta }_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma_\theta }_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma_\theta }_{\varphi \varphi } \\
{\Gamma_\varphi }_{R\varphi } & {\Gamma_\varphi }_{\theta \varphi } & {\Gamma_\varphi }_{\varphi \varphi } \\
\end{pmatrix} &= R\cos\theta \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & -\cos\theta \\ 0 & 0 & R\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta & -R\sin\theta & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\
\end{align}</math>

'''Lagrangian approach at finding a solution'''

In cylindrical coordinates, Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates exist as:

<math display="inline">\begin{cases}x = r \cos\varphi \\ y = r \sin\varphi \\ z = h \end{cases}

</math> and <math>\begin{cases} r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\\ \varphi = \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\ h = z \end{cases}</math>

Cartesian points exist and Christoffel Symbols vanish as time passes, therefore, in cylindrical coordinates:

<math>
\Gamma^r_{rr} = \Gamma^r_{\varphi r} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial z} = 0
</math>

<math>
\Gamma^r_{r \varphi} = \Gamma^r_{\varphi r} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial r}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial r}{\partial z} = - \sin \varphi \cos \varphi + \sin \varphi \cos \varphi = 0
</math>

<math>
\Gamma^r_{\varphi \varphi} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial r}{\partial z} = -\frac{x}{r} - \frac{y}{r} = -r
</math>

<math>
\Gamma^\varphi_{rr} = \Gamma^\varphi_{\varphi r} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial r^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} = 0
</math>

<math>\Gamma^\varphi_{r \varphi} = \Gamma^\varphi_{\varphi r} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial r \partial \varphi} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} = -\frac{y}{r^2} + \cos \varphi \frac{x}{r^2} = \frac{1}{r}
</math>

<math>
\Gamma^\varphi_{\varphi \varphi} = \frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial \varphi^2} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} = -\frac{x}{r^2} - \frac{y}{r^2} = 0</math>

'''Spherical coordinates (using Lagrangian 2x2x2)'''

<math>ds^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta d\phi^2</math>

The Lagrangian can be evaluated as:

<math>

L = \dot{\theta}^2 + \sin^2\theta\dot{\phi}^2</math>

Hence,

<math>\begin{cases}\ddot{\phi} + 2\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} = 0 \\ \ddot{\theta} - \sin\theta\cos\theta\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
\\ \frac{d^2x^k}{d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^k_{ij} \frac{dx^i}{d\lambda} \frac{dx^j}{d\lambda} = 0 \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\ddot{\theta}} = 0\end{cases}
</math>  can be rearranged to <math>\begin{cases}\ddot{\phi} + 2\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} = 0 \\ \ddot{\theta} - \sin\theta\cos\theta\dot{\phi}^2 = 0\end{cases} </math>

By using the following geodesic equation:

<math>\frac{d^2x^k}{d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^k_{ij} \frac{dx^i}{d\lambda} \frac{dx^j}{d\lambda} = 0

</math>  

The following can be obtained:

<math>\Gamma_{22}^1 = -\sin\theta\cos\theta(\Gamma_{12}^2) = \Gamma_{21}^2\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}</math>

<ref name=":0" />

== Lagrangian mechanics in geodesics (principles of least action in Christoffel symbols) ==
Incorporating [[Lagrangian mechanics]] and using the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]], Christoffel symbols can be substituted into the Lagrangian to account for the geometry of the manifold. Christoffel symbols being calculated from the [[Metric tensor (general relativity)|metric tensor]], the equations can be derived and expressed from the principle of least action. When applying the Euler-Lagrange equation to a system of equations, the Lagrangian will include terms involving the Christoffel symbols, allowing the equation to act for the curvature which can determine the correct equations of motion for objects moving along geodesics.

=== Using the principle of least action from the Euler-Lagrange equation ===

The Euler-Lagrange equation is applied to a functional related to the path of an object in a spherical coordinate system, 

Given <math>L\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^3)
</math> and  <math>y\in C^1[a,b]</math> such that <math>y(a)=C</math> and <math>ey(b)=d </math>

if

<math>\begin{cases} \int_{a}^{b}L(y(x))dx \\ \int_{a}^{b}L(y'(x)) dx \\ \int_{a}^{b}L(x)dx\end{cases}
</math>

Reaches its minimum <math>min\equiv y_0\in C</math> , where <math>y_0</math> is a solution that can be found by solving the differential equation:

<math>\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial y'}(y(x), y'(x))\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}(y(x), y'(x)) = 0</math>

The differential equation provides the mathematical conditions that must be satisfied for this optimal path.

<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Alexander J. Sesslar |url=https://sites.google.com/view/published-mathematical-works/home |access-date=2024-10-22 |website=sites.google.com |language=en-US}}</ref>
